claims.text: Arc melting and repeated remelting can produce chemically homogeneous bulk FeNiCrMn specimens.
The homogenized FeNiCrMn alloy will be a predominantly single-phase BCC or FCC solid solution similar to the Cantor alloy.
Room-temperature quasi-static tensile and compression testing can characterize the mechanical behavior of bulk FeNiCrMn.
Controlling strain rate, specimen geometry, and test environment will minimize extrinsic variability.
Grain boundaries mediate plastic deformation in FeNiCrMn.
Dislocation structures mediate plastic deformation in FeNiCrMn.
Potential nanoscale precipitates may mediate plastic deformation in FeNiCrMn.
The multi-principal-element solid solution in Co-free FeNiCrMn produces enhanced solid-solution strengthening.
Removing Co from the alloy modifies dislocation mobility.
The absence of Co alters the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
A Co-induced stacking-fault-energy change alters the balance between dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
Altered glide and twinning behavior changes the work-hardening rate relative to the Cantor alloy.
FeNiCrMn will exhibit yield strength and ductility distinctly different from those of the Cantor alloy.
FeNiCrMn may have higher strength because of increased lattice distortion.
Optimized dislocation interactions and grain-boundary behavior may preserve or slightly improve ductility.
Co plays a role in determining the stacking-fault energy and ductility of the Cantor alloy.
Cooling rate and homogenization conditions will influence the measured behavior.
The proposed results may apply only to as-cast or arc-melted specimens and do not establish dynamic or high-temperature behavior.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis predicts properties that differ distinctly from the Cantor alloy, but the falsification rule treats inferior properties as falsifying even though inferior properties could still constitute the predicted distinct difference.

The initial state permits a single phase similar to the Cantor alloy and the proposed mechanism relies primarily on dislocation mobility and stacking-fault energy, yet the falsification rule implies that absence of a phase-structure change can falsify the hypothesis.
